title: Checkpoint: Blues and Jazz
objective: After this level you can trace the path from spirituals and blues to bebop.
summary: About six million Black Americans left the South in the Great Migration, fleeing Jim Crow. The blues and jazz went with them, from the Deep South to Chicago and Harlem.

cards.headline: Chapter 7 finale: the music caught a train north.
cards.body: This chapter began in the South, with songs created by enslaved people. It ends in Harlem, with bebop. In between, the music traveled a long way. How did it get there? The same way millions of people did.

events.label: Spirituals and work songs pass voice to voice
The blues is a recognizable genre in the Deep South
Armstrong's Hot Five and Hot Seven make the soloist the star
The swing era's big bands fill dance floors
Bebop takes shape at Minton's Playhouse in Harlem

cards.headline: The Great Migration
cards.body: From the 1910s to 1970, about six million Black Americans left the rural South for cities in the North and West, like Chicago, Detroit and New York. They were leaving Jim Crow laws and sharecropping for more jobs, though racism was rampant in the North too. And they brought their music. Britannica notes that migrants changed the sound of the blues they carried north.

cards.headline: Jazz followed the jobs to Chicago
cards.body: During World War I, a boom in Chicago meant work for musicians, and New Orleans players went north, cornetist Joe "King" Oliver among them. In 1922 Oliver sent for Level 65's Louis Armstrong, and Armstrong made the recordings that revolutionized jazz in Chicago, between 1925 and 1928. Music moves with the people who make it.

mascot.line: Ten levels, one lesson: follow the people, and you'll find the music.

cards.headline: Chapter 7 complete
learned: How the songs of enslaved African Americans grew into the blues and jazz, then moved north with their makers.
Why a blue note falls between major and minor, and how a blues verse states a trouble twice.
What syncopation and swing do: push the melody against a beat that stays steady.
How Armstrong made the solo central, and how improvisers invent new melodies over shared chords.

questions.prompt: About how many Black Americans left the South in the Great Migration, from the 1910s to 1970?

options.label: About 60,000
options.rationale: Far more: it reshaped whole cities.

questions.explanation: About six million Black Americans moved to cities in the North and West.

questions.prompt: Why did New Orleans jazz players like King Oliver head to Chicago?

options.label: New Orleans banned jazz in 1917
options.rationale: They were drawn by work, not pushed by a ban.

options.label: A wartime boom meant jobs there
Chicago had invented the phonograph
options.rationale: The draw was jobs in a booming city.

options.label: Bebop had started there
options.rationale: Bebop came decades later, in Harlem.

questions.explanation: Chicago's wartime boom created jobs, and musicians followed; Armstrong joined Oliver there in 1922.

questions.prompt: Blues and jazz recap: Level 62's 12-bar blues also serves jazz players as what?

options.label: A chord progression, a shared map to improvise over
A dance step for the lindy hop
options.rationale: It's a chord pattern, not a dance.

options.label: A way of writing players' names on scores
options.rationale: That was Ellington's habit, not the blues form.

questions.explanation: The 12-bar blues, built on tonic, subdominant and dominant, is one of the chord maps jazz soloists improvise over.

questions.prompt: Blues and jazz recap: what did Louis Armstrong's Hot Five and Hot Seven records make central to jazz?

options.label: Collective improvisation by the whole front line
options.rationale: That's what he moved away from.

options.label: Written arrangements for big bands
options.rationale: That's Henderson and the swing era.

options.label: Silent, slow ballads
options.rationale: His records were known for virtuoso solos.

questions.explanation: Armstrong left collective improvising behind and made the virtuoso soloist preeminent.

questions.prompt: Blues and jazz recap: who first carried spirituals to audiences across the US and Europe?

options.label: The Original Dixieland Jazz Band
options.rationale: That white band made a 1917 jazz record.

options.label: Duke Ellington's Cotton Club orchestra
options.rationale: Ellington's band played jazz in Harlem from 1927.

options.label: A Fisk University student choir, the Jubilee Singers
Benny Goodman's swing band
options.rationale: Goodman led a swing band in the 1930s.

questions.explanation: The Fisk Jubilee Singers, touring from 1871 to raise money for their college, sang spirituals for audiences in the US and Europe.
